column1: // Module 00 — VS Code Walkthrough — Check on Learning

column2: According to the lessons, what makes VS Code an IDE rather than just an editor?

column3: It requires you to sign in to a Microsoft account before use
It can only be used for writing code, not plain text
It combines an editor, a terminal, and other development tools in one window
It includes a built-in AI assistant out of the box

column2: An IDE (Integrated Development Environment) bolts an editor, a terminal, and other tools together in one window so you don't have to switch between separate programs.
Which keyboard shortcut opens the VS Code command palette?

column3: Ctrl+Shift+P
Ctrl+,
Ctrl+Shift+X
Ctrl+backtick

column2: Ctrl+Shift+P (Cmd+Shift+P on Mac) opens the command palette, from which any VS Code command can be run by name.
In the VS Code window, what important information appears in the bottom-left section of the status bar?

column3: The current file's word count
The list of installed extensions
The editor font size setting
Where VS Code is connected to, such as a WSL or SSH indicator

column2: The bottom-left of the status bar shows what environment VS Code is connected to, which is where the green 'WSL: Ubuntu' or 'SSH: hostname' indicator appears.
You type echo hello into the big middle area of the VS Code window and nothing runs. What went wrong?

column3: The command needs quotes around the word hello
You typed into the editor, which stores text in a file, instead of the terminal, which runs commands
The integrated terminal only works after Docker is installed
VS Code requires commands to be run from the command palette

column2: The editor stores what you type into a file and never runs it; commands must be typed at the prompt in the terminal panel at the bottom.
Before clicking Install on an extension in the marketplace, what should you always check?

column3: That the extension was updated within the last week
That the extension is smaller than 100 MB
The publisher shown under the extension name, since multiple extensions can share the same name
That the extension has screenshots on its details page

column2: There are sometimes multiple extensions with the same name (like Python), so you must verify the publisher, such as Microsoft's ms-python, before installing.
After installing the Docker extension, its sidebar shows 'Failed to connect' or empty sections. Why?

column3: The extension was published by the wrong publisher and must be reinstalled
Docker itself is not installed yet; that happens in Module 02, so the extension has nothing to talk to
The sidebar only populates when VS Code is connected over SSH
The whale icon must be clicked twice to start the Docker service

column2: The extension is working correctly; Docker isn't installed until Module 02, so the sidebar has nothing to connect to and the empty state is expected.
What is the correct way to install WSL if wsl --status shows it is not installed?

column3: Run wsl --install in PowerShell as administrator, then reboot the computer
Install the WSL extension in VS Code, which installs WSL automatically
Run wsl --status --install in the VS Code integrated terminal
Download WSL from code.visualstudio.com and run the installer

column2: WSL is installed by running wsl --install in an administrator PowerShell, and the installation requires a reboot before Ubuntu finishes setting up.
After connecting VS Code to WSL, which command confirms your integrated terminal is really running Linux?

column3: echo hello, which prints hello back
wsl --status, which prints the default distribution
pwd, which prints the current folder
uname -a, whose output mentions Linux

column2: The lesson has you run uname -a and check that the output mentions 'Linux' as proof that the terminal is inside WSL.
When first connecting to a new SSH host, VS Code shows 'The authenticity of host ... can't be established. Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])?' What must you do?

column3: Type yes and press Enter, because pressing Enter alone does nothing
Press Enter to accept the default answer
Type the remote machine's password
Close the prompt and reconnect from the command palette

column2: The prompt has no default answer, so you must explicitly type yes and press Enter; pressing Enter by itself does nothing.
On Mac or Linux, why do you run chmod 600 on your SSH key file before connecting?

column3: It converts the key into a format VS Code can read
It registers the key with the Remote - SSH extension
SSH refuses to use keys that anyone else can read, so the permissions must be locked down
It encrypts the key with your login password

column2: chmod 600 locks down the key file's permissions so only you can read it, which SSH requires before it will accept the key.

column1: // Module 01 — Ubuntu Terminal Foundations — Check on Learning

column2: What does the command cd - do?

column3: Takes you to your previous directory and prints where it took you
Takes you to your home directory
Moves up one level to the parent directory
Takes you to the root of the filesystem

column2: cd - switches to the directory you were in previously and prints the path it moved to, letting you bounce between two locations.
What does the -p flag do in mkdir -p projects/web/app?

column3: Prompts for confirmation before creating each directory
Creates the full nested path in one command and does not error if directories already exist
Sets read and write permissions on the new directories
Prints each directory name as it is created

column2: mkdir -p creates all missing parent directories in the path and succeeds silently even if the path already exists, which makes it safe to rerun.
When redirecting echo output into a file, what is the difference between > and >>?

column3: > appends to the file while >> overwrites it
They behave exactly the same
> only works on new files and >> only works on existing files
> overwrites the file while >> appends to it

column2: A single > replaces the file's contents while >> adds to the end, which is why using > by mistake can destroy a file.
What does sudo apt update do?

column3: Installs all available package upgrades
Removes packages that are no longer needed
Downloads the latest list of available software packages
Upgrades Ubuntu to the next release version

column2: apt update only refreshes the package list so the system knows what versions are available; apt upgrade is what actually installs the upgrades.
According to the lesson, why is the gnupg package installed before Module 02?

column3: It handles encryption keys, which is needed for Docker's GPG key
It provides the certificates required for secure HTTPS connections
It is a better process viewer than top
It displays directory structures visually

column2: The lesson installs gnupg because it handles encryption keys, and the Docker installation in Module 02 requires it to work with Docker's GPG key.
After running chmod 755 hello.sh, what permission string does ls -la show for the file?

column3: -rw-r--r--
-rwxr-xr-x
-rwxrwxrwx
-rw-rw-r--

column2: 755 means the owner gets rwx (7) while group and everyone else get r-x (5), which displays as -rwxr-xr-x.
Which command shows the ports currently listening on your machine?

column3: ip a
dig +short hub.docker.com
ss -tuln

column2: ss -tuln lists listening TCP and UDP sockets with their local addresses and ports, such as port 22 for SSH.
What does systemctl is-active ssh print when the SSH service is running?

column3: enabled
running
active
online

column2: systemctl is-active gives a one-word status, and a running service reports active; enabled is what systemctl is-enabled reports for boot startup.
What does echo "hello world" | grep -v hello output?

column3: hello world
world
Nothing, because grep -v prints only lines that do NOT match
An error, because -v is not a valid grep flag

column2: The -v flag inverts the match so grep prints non-matching lines, and since the only input line contains "hello" it is excluded.
In this module, running sudo usermod -aG docker $USER fails. Why?

column3: The user does not have sudo access yet
The docker group does not exist yet; it is created when Docker is installed in Module 02
usermod can only be run while logged in directly as root
The -aG flags must come after the username

column2: The lesson runs the command as a rehearsal and it fails with "group 'docker' does not exist" because the docker group is only created when Docker is installed in Module 02.

column1: // Module 02 — Docker Installation and First Containers — Check on Learning

column2: During the setup check, you run which docker before installing anything. What result tells you that you are ready to proceed?

column3: The path /usr/bin/docker is printed
A Docker version string is printed
No output at all — Docker should not be installed yet
The message Active: active (running)

column2: The lesson expects no output from which docker, because Docker is about to be installed and any existing installation needs to be flagged first.
After running sudo usermod -aG docker $USER, docker info still fails with "permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket". What fixes this?

column3: Run newgrp docker or log out and back in to refresh group membership
Reinstall Docker Engine with sudo apt install --reinstall docker-ce
Run sudo apt update and try again
Add the docker group to /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list

column2: Group membership only takes effect in a new session, so the lesson has you run newgrp docker or log out and back in before Docker works without sudo.
Why does the installation lesson download Docker's GPG key to /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc before adding the apt repository?

column3: So you can log in to Docker Hub without a password
To prove the packages you download are really from Docker
To encrypt images that Docker pulls from the registry
So Docker commands can run without sudo

column2: The lesson explains the GPG key proves the packages you download are genuinely from Docker.
The first time you run docker run hello-world, the output starts with "Unable to find image 'hello-world:latest' locally". What does this line mean?

column3: The installation failed and Docker cannot find its own files
You typed the image name wrong and need to retry
The Docker daemon is not running and must be started
It is not an error — Docker did not have the image cached, so it pulled it from Docker Hub

column2: The lesson stresses this line is not an error: Docker checked locally, found nothing, and pulled the image from Docker Hub before running it.
You ran docker run hello-world twice, but docker ps shows nothing. Why?

column3: The containers were automatically deleted when they finished
docker ps only shows running containers, and the hello-world containers exited; docker ps -a shows them
hello-world runs entirely in memory and never creates a container
You need sudo to see containers with docker ps

column2: By default docker ps lists only running containers; the exited hello-world containers are still on disk and appear with docker ps -a.
In the command docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web nginx, what does -p 8080:80 do?

column3: Forwards port 8080 on your machine to port 80 inside the container
Forwards port 80 on your machine to port 8080 inside the container
Makes nginx listen on both ports 8080 and 80 inside the container
Limits the container to 8080 KB of memory on port 80

column2: The lesson explains -p 8080:80 maps host port 8080 to container port 80, where nginx listens, so you reach it at localhost:8080.
Which command opens an interactive shell inside the running container named web?

column3: docker shell web
docker run -it web bash
docker exec -it web bash
docker logs -f web

column2: The lesson uses docker exec -it web bash to get a shell inside the running container; the prompt changes to root inside the container's filesystem.
What is the difference between docker rm and docker rmi?

column3: docker rm removes running containers; docker rmi removes stopped ones
docker rm removes an image; docker rmi removes a container
They are aliases and do exactly the same thing
docker rm removes a container; docker rmi removes an image

column2: As the lesson's quick reference states, docker rm <name> removes a stopped container while docker rmi <image> removes an image.
What does docker container prune -f do?

column3: Stops all running containers
Removes all stopped containers in one step
Removes all images not used by any container
Removes both containers and their images

column2: The lesson introduces docker container prune -f as the shortcut that removes all stopped containers at once; images require docker image prune -a.
According to the VS Code Docker sidebar lesson, which task is better done with the CLI than the sidebar?

column3: Running a container with specific port mappings and a custom name
Seeing what is running right now at a glance
Inspecting a container's environment variables and mounts
Opening a container's logs in an editor tab

column2: The lesson's comparison table says the sidebar's Run option loses control over flags like -p and --name, so running with specific port mappings is better in the CLI.
